scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: I'm covering the monitoring desk today. An alert
popped up in the night and then cleared itself, and the ops chat is clear
about what it was: one of the big middle routers -- they keep writing "R6",
one message says maybe "R7" -- crashed, and everything going through the
middle is falling into a hole. Half the screens look normal to me, but I am
not going to second-guess the ops people, and I've been told to get this
looked at urgently. So: one of your middle boxes died. Check it and sort it
out today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is an IP address misconfiguration on r1's eth0 interface. R1 and R2 are directly connected over collision domain A (r1.eth0, r2.eth0), and R2.eth0 is correctly configured with `1.1.1.2/8` in the `1.0.0.0/8` subnet. However, r1.eth0 carries `12.1.1.1/8` — a completely different /8 network. Because the two interface addresses lie in non-overlapping subnets (1.0.0.0/8 vs 12.0.0.0/8), OSPF on FRR refuses to accept each other's hello packets (the network-mask consistency check fails), so no adjacency ever forms on segment A. Both routers show exactly 0 neighbours on their segment-A interfaces, confirmed directly by `show ip ospf interface` output on both devices.

The practical impact is that the intended direct R1↔R2 transit link is a complete black hole: neither router can reach the other's eth0 IP at the data plane, and no OSPF link-state information is exchanged over it. All traffic between R1 and R2 is instead detoured three hops through R3 (cost 30 vs the expected direct cost 10), as seen in both routing tables. A spurious `12.0.0.0/8` prefix is also injected into OSPF from r1 and propagated network-wide. The ops alert likely triggered when ospfd on r1 restarted (watchfrr is running), causing a brief OSPF reconvergence; it cleared when the daemon came back up, but the underlying misconfiguration remained.

Root cause: r1.eth0 has been assigned `12.1.1.1/8` instead of the correct `1.1.1.1/8`, with a matching incorrect OSPF network statement (`network 12.0.0.0/8 area 0` instead of `network 1.0.0.0/8 area 0`).

Corrective fix: On r1, change the interface address from `12.1.1.1/8` to `1.1.1.1/8`, and update the OSPF configuration to `network 1.0.0.0/8 area 0` (removing `network 12.0.0.0/8 area 0`). This will allow R1 and R2 to form a Full OSPF adjacency on segment A, restore the direct transit link, and withdraw the spurious 12.0.0.0/8 prefix from the OSPF domain.
